message:
QUESTION:
Did the 1 June move to a new content delivery network (CDN) improve the site's conversion rate, and what is a faster site worth?

DATA:
An online retailer migrated its website to a new content delivery network (CDN) on 1 June. Two weeks before (18-31 May) vs two weeks after (1-14 June):

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June |
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 |
| Median page load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s |
| 95th-percentile page load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% |

Conversion = orders / sessions. Page load times come from real-user monitoring across all page views.

Same two calendar periods last year, when there were no site or infrastructure changes: conversion 2.4% (18-31 May) and 2.6% (1-14 June).

The retailer's conversion rate rises every year in early June when the summer ranges launch. This year the summer ranges again launched on 1 June. No other site changes were made between 18 May and 14 June.

KNOWN FLAWS:
F1. [calculation] The reduction is (7.5 − 4.8) / 7.5 = 36%. 56% comes from dividing the 2.7 s fall by the new value (4.8). The draft's claim that the slowest experiences 'improved even more' than the median (34%) is barely true at 36%. CORRECTION: 95th percentile fell by 36%, similar to the median's 34%.
F2. [misreport] The data show bounce rate fell from 48% to 44%. CORRECTION: A 4-point (8% relative) fall in bounce rate.
F3. [method] Ignores the seasonal baseline: the same calendar periods last year, with no site changes, show the same 0.2-point rise (2.4% to 2.6%) from the summer range launch, which happened again on 1 June. CORRECTION: Year-over-year difference-in-differences: (2.70 − 2.50) − (2.6 − 2.4) = 0.0 points. There is no detectable conversion effect of the CDN.
F4. [inference] Derives a linear causal 'value per second' from one confounded before/after comparison and extrapolates it beyond the observed range. CORRECTION: The data support no value-per-second estimate (the seasonally adjusted effect is about zero). A randomised latency experiment would be needed.

EXTENSIONS:
- Run a statistical check on the raw conversion change (2.50% vs 2.70%, z of about 4) and contrast it with the seasonally adjusted comparison, showing that a highly significant before/after change can be entirely seasonal.
- Check whether the sessions increase (+5%) is also seasonal, using last year's session counts for the same periods, which the analyst should request.
- Segment by device or connection type: speed gains typically matter most on mobile and slow connections, so an effect masked in the aggregate could appear there (data would be needed).

FINAL VERSION:
# Review of the CDN analysis (third pass)

## Arithmetic re-checked

Almost every figure holds: conversion 2.50% → 2.70%, the 250 + 420 order split, SE 0.049 pts, combined ±0.16 pts, the proportional rounding range of −0.12 to +0.10 pts, 15 orders a day per 0.1 pts, all three holdout sizes, and the 170-order holdout cost. Two figures are wrong:

| Item | Stated | Correct |
|---|---|---|
| Bounce rate without 10,000 extra bounce sessions | ≈ 43% | 92,400 − 10,000 = 82,400 bounces ÷ 200,000 = **≈ 41%**. This makes the review's point stronger. |
| 20% holdout, 0.2 pts | 61,000–64,000 | **≈ 61,000** at June rates (holdout 2.5%, rest 2.7%). The 64,000 figure assumes the faster arm converts *worse*, which is the wrong direction. |

## Remaining problems

1. **The holdout is described as precise, but it barely beats the existing estimate.** A 4-week, 20% holdout at June traffic gives a 95% interval of about **±0.12 pts**. The current observational estimate is ±0.16 pts. The holdout's real advantage is that it is free of the seasonal bias, not that it is more precise.
   - Power to detect a 0.1-point effect is only about **30%**.
   - So a "no significant effect" result would not rule out about 5,500 orders a year.
   - The report should present the result as a confidence interval, not a pass/fail test.
   - The test should be sized against a break-even effect, which the report never defines.
2. **The uncertainty statements contradict each other.**
   - The short answer says "at least ±0.2".
   - Section 3 says −0.2 to +0.2 "fits the data", then says only effects "above 0.3" are unlikely.
   - Section 4 uses a prior range up to 0.28.
   - The fix is one consistent hierarchy: a quantified ±0.16, about ±0.2–0.3 once the unquantified terms are included, and effects above about 0.3 hard to reconcile with the data.
3. **"Compare orders per day year on year" repeats the original mistake.** A raw year-on-year comparison of orders includes business growth. It needs the same January–May baseline adjustment as conversion. It also only avoids the tag-timing problem if orders come from the order system, not from analytics.
4. **The conclusion overclaims the speed-up.** Section 1 says the page mix changed at the launch, which could bias the speed-up in either direction. The conclusion still says "probably by more than measured". Only the bias from missing monitoring data is clearly conservative.
5. **"What is a faster site worth" is only half answered.**
   - The delay test values the 1.1 s already gained. Further speed-ups from a 2.1 s base will probably be worth less per second, so the per-second figure should not be extrapolated.
   - The value formula leaves out one-off migration costs.
   - A break-even threshold would turn the formula into a decision rule.
6. **The timing advice is too even-handed.** Injecting delays during Black Friday risks the highest-value traffic of the year. Peak shoppers are also untypical, and many retailers freeze changes during peak. January should be the default. In January both traffic and the absolute effect will probably be lower, so the test will probably need longer than 4 weeks, not just a recalculation.

---

# Improved version

# CDN migration: the site got faster, but the effect on sales has not been measured yet

**Short answer**
- **Did the CDN raise conversion?** These data cannot tell.
  - Conversion rose 0.20 points.
  - Last year, with no site changes, it also rose about 0.2 points over the same dates, because of the summer range launch.
  - The best estimate of the CDN's effect is about zero.
  - The quantified 95% uncertainty is ±0.16 points. Realistically it is ±0.2–0.3 points, because some sources of error cannot yet be measured.
- **What is a faster site worth?** Not yet known.
  - Each 0.1 points of conversion is worth about 15 orders a day at early-June traffic, or roughly 5,500 orders a year.
  - Published figures imply 0.05–0.28 points for a speed-up of this size. That is up to about 15,000 orders a year.
  - Whether that matters depends on the break-even effect in Section 4.
- **How to find out**
  - Start with a year-on-year comparison using the five months of data already collected. It costs almost nothing.
  - Then run a visitor-level holdout in January, sized against the break-even effect.

### 1. Speed: a large improvement, probably caused by the CDN

| | 18–31 May | 1–14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s | −1.1 s (−34%) |
| 95th-percentile load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s | −2.7 s (−36%) |

No other site change was made, so the CDN is the likely cause. Two caveats pull in different directions:
- **Page views abandoned before the monitoring script ran are missing.** The old CDN probably lost more slow loads this way, so this bias makes the measured speed-up *conservative*.
- **The figures are weighted by page view, and the page mix changed at the launch.** This bias could go either way.

To confirm the gain, compare like-for-like page types (product, basket, checkout), split by device.

### 2. Traffic, orders and engagement

| | 18–31 May | 1–14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 | +5% |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 | +13% (357 → 405 a day) |
| Conversion | 2.50% | 2.70% | +0.20 pts (+8%) |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% | −4 pts |

Of the 670 extra orders, about 250 come from more traffic and about 420 from higher conversion. Launches normally raise traffic and engagement. Last year's sessions, orders and bounce rate for these dates are not available, so none of this can be credited to the CDN.

**Measurement check.** A faster site may have started recording visitors who previously left before the analytics tag fired. That would add low-intent sessions and *depress* measured conversion. The falling bounce rate does not rule this out. Even if all 10,000 extra sessions were new bounces, the bounce rate without them would be about 41%, still a fall that the launch could explain. Two checks are needed:
- Confirm that the migration did not change how the analytics tag is served or how sessions are defined.
- Compare **orders per day from the order system** year on year, adjusted by the January–May year-on-year gap. This adjustment is needed because orders also include business growth.

### 3. Conversion: no detectable effect, wide margin of error

| | 18–31 May | 1–14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| This year (CDN + launch) | 2.50% | 2.70% | +0.20 pts (+8.0%) |
| Last year (launch only) | 2.4% | 2.6% | +0.2 pts (≈ +8.3%, rounded) |
| **Implied CDN effect** | | | **≈ 0 pts** |

| Source of uncertainty | Size (95%) |
|---|---|
| Sampling noise, both years | ±0.14 pts, if last year's traffic was similar |
| Rounding of last year's figures | −0.12 to +0.10 pts, applying last year's percentage lift because the base rates differ |
| **Quantified total** | **±0.16 pts** |
| Repeat visitors, day-to-day variation | Widens the range; not yet measured |
| Year-to-year variation in the June lift | Unknown, because only one earlier year is available. This is possibly the largest term. |
| Newly recorded low-intent sessions | Would bias the estimate *downward*; size unknown |

**Reading the range.** Effects within about ±0.16 points fit the data comfortably. Once the unmeasured terms are added, a realistic range is ±0.2–0.3 points. Effects above about 0.3 points are hard to reconcile with the data, but only if last year was a typical year.

Published figures, mostly from vendors, suggest a 1-second speed-up raises conversion by a few percent to about 10%. Here that would be 0.05–0.28 points, which sits inside this range. **This comparison cannot detect a realistic speed effect, and it cannot rule one out.**

### 4. What a faster site is worth

Two questions need to be kept apart:
- **The value of speed.** A faster site is very unlikely to *lower* conversion. Combining the published figures with the data's upper limit gives a plausible range of 0 to about 0.25–0.28 points.
- **The CDN's total effect.** This can be negative even if speed helps. Examples are bot protection blocking real customers, stale cached prices or stock, and assets failing in some regions. Check error rates and challenge rates by region.

At early-June traffic of about 15,000 sessions a day:

| Speed effect | Orders a day | Orders a year (at early-June traffic) |
|---|---|---|
| +0.1 pts | 15 | ≈ 5,500 |
| +0.2 pts | 30 | ≈ 11,000 |
| +0.28 pts | 42 | ≈ 15,000 |

Recalculate these from actual annual sessions, because early June may not be typical.

**Valuation.** Use only the *incremental* conversion caused by speed. Do not use the raw change before and after the migration, because that includes the summer launch.

> Annual value ≈ annual sessions × Δconversion (from speed) × AOV × contribution margin
> + any speed-caused change in traffic or AOV × margin
> − change in annual CDN cost − amortised one-off migration cost

**Break-even effect.** This is the conversion lift at which the migration pays for itself:

> Δconversion (break-even) = (Δ annual CDN cost + amortised migration cost) ÷ (annual sessions × AOV × margin)

This number decides how precise any test needs to be. If the break-even effect is well below 0.1 points, the migration very probably pays, and a test matters mainly for future speed investments.

The test measures the value of the 1.1 s already gained. Further speed-ups from a 2.1 s base will probably be worth less per second. If the effect is near zero, judge the migration on cost, reliability under peak load and SEO.

### 5. How to measure it

1. **Year-on-year comparison over a longer period (now, almost free)**
   - Compare June–October conversion **and** orders per day from the order system with the same months last year. Subtract the January–May year-on-year gap.
   - Sampling noise falls to about ±0.05 points. The bigger risks are that the pre-migration gap does not stay constant and that other changes after June also affect the result, such as pricing, marketing or releases.
   - List those changes, and treat the result as supporting evidence, not proof.

2. **Segment comparison (cheap)**
   - Compare the change in conversion where speed improved a lot with where it improved a little, by region, device or connection type.
   - This only removes the seasonal effect if the summer lift is similar across segments. Check that against last year's segment data first.

3. **Holdout test (removes the bias; measures the value of speed)**
   - **Design.** Assign 20% of *visitors*, by cookie, device ID or login, to the old CDN. Alternatively, inject delays that reproduce the old load-time *distribution* by page type (about +1.1 s at the median and +2.7 s at the 95th percentile). Analyse results at visitor level.
   - **Precision at June rates:**
     - 4 weeks gives about **±0.12 points**.
     - Power is about 90% for 0.2 points and about 30% for 0.1 points.
     - Detecting 0.1 points needs about 11–12 weeks at 20%, or about 7–8 weeks split 50/50.
     - Repeat visitors increase all of these.
     - Choose the size from the break-even effect, and report the confidence interval rather than "significant / not significant".
   - **Timing.** Run it in **January**. Black Friday (27 November) is two weeks away, so a test started now would run into peak. A peak-season test would put delays on the most valuable traffic of the year, give results that are untypical, and probably conflict with a change freeze. January traffic and conversion will be lower, so the test will probably need more than 4 weeks. Recalculate with January figures.
   - **Cost.** About 170 lost orders over 4 weeks at June traffic if the effect is 0.2 points; roughly 40–240 across the plausible range.
   - **Do not plan a 5% holdout.** It would need about 9 months to detect 0.1 points.

4. **Better baselines.** Pull unrounded sessions, orders, conversion, bounce rate and device mix for last year and earlier years, plus the dates of launch marketing and promotions. This shows how much the June lift varies from year to year.

A model linking load time to conversion within a single period does not show cause and effect. Slow sessions differ from fast ones in device, connection and location.

### 6. Next steps

1. Do not use a per-second conversion figure in business cases until one has been measured here.
2. Check the analytics tag and session configuration, and CDN error and challenge rates by region.
3. Calculate the break-even effect using AOV, margin and CDN costs.
4. Run the adjusted year-on-year comparison, using conversion and order-system orders, and the segment comparison.
5. Plan the January holdout, sized against the break-even effect.
6. Record the CDN's cost, uptime and performance through peak.
7. In future, do not release infrastructure changes on seasonal launch dates, or release them to a split of traffic.

**Conclusion.** The migration made the site about a third faster. The 0.2-point rise in conversion matches the usual summer lift, so there is no evidence yet that speed increased sales. The data are also too coarse to show that it did not. If published effects hold here, the upside is up to about 15,000 orders a year. Whether that justifies the migration depends on a break-even calculation that needs AOV, margin and cost. The five months of post-migration data and a January holdout sized against that break-even can settle the question.
